spawn_spec.prompt:
Deep engineering research on **injecting per-user memory into LLM prompts without wrecking cost, latency, or caching**. Cite every claim with a URL; mark DOCUMENTED vs INFERRED.

Context: a Next.js app calling OpenAI (gpt-5.x era), using both chat.completions and the Responses API with response chaining (previous_response_id / stored responses). It wants to inject a per-professor memory block into many different system prompts.

Answer precisely:
1. **Prompt caching mechanics**: OpenAI automatic prompt caching - exact rules (minimum prefix length, what invalidates a cache hit, how the cached prefix is matched, TTL, how `cached_tokens` is reported, discount rate). Same for Anthropic explicit cache_control breakpoints if relevant as a contrast. State precisely where a variable memory block MUST be placed to preserve caching, and quantify the cost impact of getting it wrong.
2. **Responses API + memory**: how `previous_response_id` chaining interacts with a system prompt that changes between turns; whether instructions can be updated mid-chain; what happens to cached/stored context; whether injecting new memory mid-conversation is even possible without breaking the chain. Find the actual API semantics in OpenAI docs.
3. **Selection without embeddings**: practical, defensible heuristics for choosing which N memory records to inject for a given task type when the total corpus is small (tens of records per user) - scope filters, task-type tagging, recency, usage counts, explicit pinning. Any published engineering write-ups or framework implementations doing non-vector selection. Compare against just injecting all of them.
4. **Token budget enforcement in code**: how to measure and cap injected memory tokens server-side (tokenizer choice for gpt-5.x, js-tiktoken/gpt-tokenizer accuracy, cheap approximations), and what to do on overflow (drop by priority, compact, error).
5. **Ordering and placement effects**: evidence on where in the prompt persistent instructions should go (top of system vs just before the user turn), interaction with lost-in-the-middle, and whether repeating critical constraints at the end is worth the tokens.
6. **Observability**: what to log per call so you can later answer 'which memory items were in this prompt and did they change the output' - and how teams actually do counterfactual with/without-memory runs cheaply in production (sampling rates, cost).

Deliverable: a concrete engineering spec with numbers, plus a list of mistakes that silently cost money or break caching. Do not write our application code.

# Engineering spec: per-user memory without destroying caching

**Research snapshot:** 2026-08-11. OpenAI’s caching behavior now differs between models before GPT-5.6 and GPT-5.6-and-later, so do not treat “GPT-5.x” as one cache regime. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)

**Labels**

- **DOCUMENTED**: explicitly stated by a cited vendor, framework, or published paper.
- **INFERRED**: an engineering recommendation derived from documented behavior; validate with application evals.

---

## 1. Prompt caching mechanics

### OpenAI automatic caching

- **DOCUMENTED — Eligibility:** automatic caching applies when the rendered prompt contains at least **1,024 input tokens**. Requests below that still return `cached_tokens`, but it is zero. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED — Match rule:** only an **exact prompt-prefix match** can hit. Static instructions, examples, tools, images, and their ordering must be identical. Variable content belongs after the common prefix. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED — Granularity:** OpenAI reports cacheable matched lengths beginning at 1,024 tokens and increasing in **128-token increments**. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED — Routing:** OpenAI routes requests based on a hash of the prompt prefix; `prompt_cache_key` is combined with the prefix hash and can improve routing for requests sharing a prefix. On GPT-5.6 and later, setting it is required for the newer, more reliable matching behavior. OpenAI recommends roughly **15 requests/minute or less per key**, sharding higher-volume traffic across keys. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED — What invalidates the reusable suffix:** any token difference before or inside a would-be cached prefix—including whitespace, JSON serialization, tool order, image details, examples, timestamps, memory ordering, or instruction revisions—ends the exact match at that point. Content after the first difference can no longer belong to that shared prefix. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) [OpenAI caching cookbook](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/prompt_caching101)
- **DOCUMENTED — Scope:** cache entries are organization-scoped, not shared across organizations. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED — Reporting:**
  - Responses API: `usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens`.
  - Chat Completions: `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`.
  - GPT-5.6+ also reports writes as `cache_write_tokens`.  
  [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED — Latency:** OpenAI reports up to an **80% latency reduction** for long prompts over approximately 10,000 tokens, but this is not a per-request SLA. [OpenAI caching cookbook](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/prompt_caching101)

### OpenAI retention and write-price split

- **DOCUMENTED — Models before GPT-5.6, in-memory:** entries generally survive **5–10 minutes of inactivity**, may remain for as long as **one hour**, and can be evicted. Manual clearing is unavailable. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED — Older-model extended retention:** supported models can use `prompt_cache_retention: "24h"`; extended retention can keep prefixes up to 24 hours. The exact supported policy is model-dependent. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED — GPT-5.6+:** cached prefixes remain eligible for at least **30 minutes** and may remain longer; `prompt_cache_options.ttl` expresses a minimum lifetime rather than selecting the older maximum-retention policy. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED — Writes:**
  - Before GPT-5.6: cache writes have no additional fee beyond ordinary uncached input.
  - GPT-5.6+: writes cost **1.25x** ordinary uncached input and are reported separately.  
  [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)

### Discount rate and concrete cost

Cached-input prices are model-specific rather than a universal contractual percentage.

- **DOCUMENTED — GPT-5:** ordinary input is **$1.25/M tokens** and cached input **$0.125/M**, a **90% discount**. [GPT-5 model pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5)
- **DOCUMENTED — GPT-5.4 example:** ordinary input is **$2.50/M** and cached input **$0.25/M**, also a **90% discount**. [GPT-5.4 model pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.4)
- **INFERRED — Cost of a misplaced memory block:** if a varying memory record appears before an otherwise reusable 8,000-token prefix:
  - GPT-5 loses `8,000 × ($1.25-$0.125)/1M = $0.009` per repeat, or **$9 per 1,000 calls**.
  - GPT-5.4 loses `8,000 × ($2.50-$0.25)/1M = $0.018` per repeat, or **$18 per 1,000 calls**.  
  This excludes output costs and GPT-5.6+ cache-write charges. Pricing sources: [GPT-5](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5), [GPT-5.4](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.4).

### Required placement

Use this logical ordering:

```text
[stable platform/developer policy]
[stable task-specific prompt version]
[stable examples and tool definitions]
[variable per-user memory block]
[current user input]
```

- **INFERRED — Hard placement rule:** the memory block **MUST come after every token you intend to share across users or calls**. Otherwise the first per-user difference truncates the reusable prefix. This follows directly from exact-prefix matching. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **INFERRED:** serialize selected memories deterministically: stable field order, stable record ordering, no current timestamp, and no request-specific prose before them.
- **INFERRED:** use a cache key based on the reusable prefix, for example `task:<template-id>:<template-version>`, not a random request ID. Include `user_id` only if traffic intentionally reuses a user-specific prefix; excessive cardinality reduces useful reuse. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **INFERRED:** because there are many distinct system prompts, caching occurs independently per task-template prefix. A common memory block cannot magically be reused after several different preceding prompts: prefix caches are not substring caches.
- **INFERRED:** do not move memory ahead of the task prompt merely to cache memory across task types. That makes each task prompt an uncached suffix and may weaken instruction structure. Prefer caching the usually longer, higher-fanout task template across users.

### Anthropic contrast: explicit breakpoints

- **DOCUMENTED:** Anthropic supports `cache_control` breakpoints. A breakpoint hashes the full prefix through the marked block; changing anything at or before it produces a different hash. [Anthropic prompt caching](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED:** Anthropic allows up to **four cache breakpoints**. Cache lookup can walk backward at most **20 content blocks per breakpoint** to find a prefix written by an earlier request. [Anthropic prompt caching](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED:** default TTL is **5 minutes**; an explicit **1-hour** TTL is available. Hits refresh the relevant lifetime. [Anthropic prompt caching](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED — Pricing multipliers:** 5-minute writes cost **1.25x**, one-hour writes **2x**, and reads **0.1x** base input price. [Anthropic pricing](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/pricing)
- **DOCUMENTED:** minimum cacheable length is model-dependent; under-threshold marked content is processed normally without an error, so usage fields must be checked. [Anthropic prompt caching](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)
- **INFERRED:** for Anthropic, place an explicit breakpoint on the last stable task-prompt block, immediately before per-user memory. Do not mark the changing memory or current user block as the only breakpoint.

---

## 2. Responses API chaining and changing memory

### Actual API semantics

- **DOCUMENTED:** `previous_response_id` links a new response to a previous response and creates threaded, multi-turn context. It cannot be combined with a `conversation` parameter. [OpenAI conversation state](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state) [OpenAI Node response types](https://github.com/openai/openai-node/blob/master/src/resources/responses/responses.ts)
- **DOCUMENTED:** the `instructions` value from the previous response **is not carried over** when `previous_response_id` is used. A new call can therefore replace the system/developer instructions while retaining the conversational chain. [OpenAI Node response types](https://github.com/openai/openai-node/blob/master/src/resources/responses/responses.ts#L1020-L1027)
- **DOCUMENTED:** all previous input tokens represented by the response chain are still billed as input on later calls, even though the application does not resend them verbatim. Chaining is state management, not free context. [OpenAI conversation state](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state)
- **DOCUMENTED:** response storage and prompt caching are separate mechanisms. Stored responses provide retrievable/threaded state; `cached_tokens` reports model-prefix cache reuse. [OpenAI conversation state](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state) [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)

### Consequences for memory

- **INFERRED — Updating memory is possible without breaking the chain:** continue sending `previous_response_id`, but supply the complete current instruction set, including the newly selected memory, on every turn where it should apply. The response chain remains intact because instructions are explicitly replaceable. [OpenAI Node response types](https://github.com/openai/openai-node/blob/master/src/resources/responses/responses.ts#L1020-L1027)
- **INFERRED:** if memory is embedded in `instructions`, do not assume prior memory remains active. This replacement behavior is desirable: corrected or deleted memory does not have to accumulate as another instruction.
- **INFERRED:** if memory is instead sent as an ordinary `input` item, it becomes part of the threaded input history and can remain semantically visible on subsequent turns. Repeated updates can then leave contradictory old and new memory in the chain. Use replaceable `instructions` for authoritative current state.
- **INFERRED — Caching tradeoff:** changing an `instructions` prefix can reduce prompt-cache reuse for context after that change. Keep the stable policy/template bytes first and the memory suffix last inside the rendered instruction content, or use a later developer input item where your API/model supports the desired hierarchy. Verify actual `cached_tokens`; do not infer hits from `previous_response_id`.
- **INFERRED — Start a new chain only when:** previous turns themselves contain sensitive, deleted, or materially contradictory memory that must no longer be visible; a context reset is semantically desired; or measurements show chain growth is more expensive than resending a compacted transcript.

---

## 3. Memory selection without embeddings

For tens of records per professor, deterministic filtering is defensible and easier to audit than introducing a vector store.

### Record schema

**INFERRED:** maintain at least:

```text
id
user_id / professor_id
scope                 // global, course, class, assignment, student, task
scope_id
task_tags[]
kind                  // preference, policy, fact, constraint, style
priority              // critical, high, normal, low
pinned
effective_at
expires_at
updated_at
last_used_at
use_count
status/version
text
```

Structured profiles are a published non-vector memory pattern: LangMem maintains a concise typed profile, isolates it with a user namespace, and can update one profile in place rather than inserting unlimited facts. [LangMem user profiles](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langmem/guides/manage_user_profile/)

Letta likewise distinguishes attached, in-context memory blocks that are pinned into the system prompt from out-of-context history. [Letta memory](https://docs.letta.com/guides/agents/memory/)

### Deterministic selector

1. **DOCUMENTED pattern / INFERRED policy:** isolate by `user_id`; framework memory stores use user-specific namespaces for this purpose. [LangMem user profiles](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langmem/guides/manage_user_profile/)
2. **INFERRED:** discard expired, deleted, disabled, wrong-tenant, and wrong-scope records.
3. **INFERRED:** include applicable pinned/critical records first.
4. **INFERRED:** require either:
   - a matching task tag, or
   - a global tag explicitly allowed for all task types.
5. **INFERRED:** rank the remainder lexicographically, not with a mysterious blended score:
   1. exact scope match,
   2. task-tag specificity,
   3. priority,
   4. most recently updated,
   5. most recently used,
   6. descending use count,
   7. stable ID as tie-breaker.
6. **INFERRED:** greedily admit records while the memory token budget remains.
7. **INFERRED:** log exclusions and reasons, especially `wrong_scope`, `wrong_task`, `expired`, and `token_budget`.

Lexicographic ranking prevents a frequently used but irrelevant global note from beating an exact assignment-level rule merely because of an arbitrary numeric weight.

### Recommended limits

- **INFERRED starting point:** cap ordinary selected records at **8**, plus applicable pinned records, and cap the final serialized memory block at **800 tokens**.
- **INFERRED:** allow a higher ceiling, such as **1,200 tokens**, only for tasks whose evals demonstrate a benefit, not as a global default.
- **INFERRED:** enforce both count and token caps. A count-only cap fails when one record contains several paragraphs.

### Against injecting everything

Example: 30 records averaging 50 tokens produce approximately **1,500 memory tokens** before wrappers.

- **INFERRED — GPT-5 uncached input:** `1,500 × $1.25/M = $0.001875/call`, or **$1.875/1,000 calls**. [GPT-5 pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5)
- **INFERRED — In a 10-turn Responses chain:** if that context is billed on every subsequent turn, the accumulated input exposure is substantially larger than a single 1,500-token injection. [OpenAI conversation state](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state)
- **DOCUMENTED:** long-context models often retrieve information best near the beginning or end and significantly worse from the middle. More irrelevant memories can therefore hurt effective use even before the context limit is reached. [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)
- **INFERRED:** “inject all” is acceptable only when the complete serialized corpus remains below the chosen budget, all records are relevant to every task, and A/B evals show no quality regression.

---

## 4. Server-side token enforcement

### Tokenizer

- **DOCUMENTED:** OpenAI’s `tiktoken` provides `encoding_for_model()` and `o200k_base`; modern GPT-4o-era models use the `o200k_base` family. [tiktoken](https://github.com/openai/tiktoken) [OpenAI token-counting cookbook](https://github.com/openai/openai-cookbook/blob/main/examples/How_to_count_tokens_with_tiktoken.ipynb)
- **DOCUMENTED:** `js-tiktoken` is a pure-JavaScript port, while `tiktoken` provides WASM bindings with feature parity to the Python implementation. [JS tiktoken](https://github.com/dqbd/tiktoken)
- **DOCUMENTED:** `gpt-tokenizer` advertises GPT-5 support and maps modern GPT models to `o200k_base`; it is third-party rather than OpenAI-maintained. [gpt-tokenizer](https://github.com/niieani/gpt-tokenizer)
- **INFERRED recommendation:** on a Next.js Node runtime, prefer `tiktoken`/`js-tiktoken` with the model mapping supported by the installed package. If a just-released model alias is unknown, explicitly fall back to `o200k_base`, record that fallback, and compare estimated tokens to API usage.
- **INFERRED:** tokenize the **exact serialized memory block**, including IDs or XML/JSON delimiters sent to the model. Counting only database text underestimates the prompt.

Tokenizers can count the text accurately for their encoding, but model/API message framing and future model mappings may differ.

- **INFERRED:** retain a safety reserve of **32 tokens or 5%, whichever is larger**, for memory wrappers and serialization drift.
- **INFERRED:** calibrate periodically using:
  `actual total input - known non-memory input`
  versus the local estimate. OpenAI usage is the billing source of truth. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)

### Cheap approximation

- **DOCUMENTED:** tiktoken notes that one token averages about **four bytes** in English, but tokenization is language- and content-dependent. [tiktoken README](https://github.com/openai/tiktoken)
- **INFERRED:** `characters / 4` is suitable only as a quick prefilter. For a hard budget, use the tokenizer; IDs, JSON, code, non-Latin text, and punctuation can differ substantially.
- **INFERRED:** a safe two-stage path is:
  1. reject obviously oversized candidates using `UTF-8 bytes / 3`,
  2. run exact BPE counting before the API call.

### Overflow policy

1. **INFERRED:** never drop mandatory safety or pinned policy records silently.
2. **INFERRED:** remove lowest-ranked ordinary records until under budget.
3. **INFERRED:** if one ordinary record exceeds the remaining budget, skip it rather than truncating it mid-sentence.
4. **INFERRED:** use a stored, versioned compact form only if it was generated earlier and reviewed/evaluated. Do not make a summarization call on every request; that adds latency, output cost, and nondeterminism.
5. **INFERRED:** if pinned records alone exceed the cap, fail closed with an internal configuration error. Automatically truncating authoritative policy can silently change behavior.
6. **INFERRED:** expose counters for `memory_overflow`, `records_dropped`, and `pinned_over_budget`.

---

## 5. Ordering and placement effects

Two distinct concerns must be balanced:

1. cacheable static material should be first;
2. immediately relevant context/query often benefits from recency.

- **DOCUMENTED:** OpenAI explicitly recommends static content at the beginning and variable/user-specific content at the end for cache hits. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED:** long-context retrieval performance is commonly U-shaped: strongest at the beginning and end, weaker in the middle. [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)
- **DOCUMENTED:** Anthropic reports that placing long-form documents before the query can improve quality by up to **30%** in complex multi-document tests. [Anthropic long-context tips](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/long-context-tips)

### Recommended order

```text
1. Stable, authoritative platform/developer constraints
2. Stable task definition and output contract
3. Stable examples/tools
4. Selected per-user memory, clearly delimited as contextual data
5. Current user request
```

- **INFERRED:** put universal persistent instructions at the **top**, not only immediately before the user. They receive the strongest structural position and remain cacheable.
- **INFERRED:** put selected memory near the **end**, immediately before the user request. This preserves the stable prefix and avoids burying relevant memory in the middle.
- **INFERRED:** label memory as contextual facts/preferences, not as text allowed to override platform or task policy.
- **INFERRED:** order records inside the memory block with pinned/critical first and exact task-specific records last. This gives critical material primacy and task-relevant material recency.

### Repeating critical constraints

- **INFERRED:** do not repeat the full policy at the end by default. It adds uncached tokens and can create conflicting duplicate wording.
- **INFERRED:** repeat only a short, machine-stable sentinel for a constraint that fails measurable evals—for example, a one-line output-format reminder immediately before the user input.
- **INFERRED:** repetition is worthwhile only when the measured reduction in violation cost exceeds:
  `repeated_tokens × uncached_input_price × call_volume`.
- **INFERRED:** never generate the repeated reminder dynamically; changing wording would impair prefix consistency and observability.

---

## 6. Observability and counterfactuals

### Log one structured record per model call

**INFERRED required fields:**

```text
request_id, trace_id, timestamp
user_hash / professor_hash
conversation_id, previous_response_id, response_id
API surface and model snapshot
task_type
prompt_template_id + version/hash
memory_selector_version
memory_budget_tokens
candidate_count
selected memory IDs + record versions
selected order
per-item estimated tokens
total memory estimated tokens
excluded IDs + exclusion reasons
pinned IDs
memory-block content hash
prompt_cache_key
input_tokens, cached_tokens, cache_write_tokens
output_tokens, reasoning tokens if supplied
latency_ms, time_to_first_token_ms
status/error
sampling/experiment cohort
output hash or encrypted output reference
downstream outcome and evaluator scores
```

- **DOCUMENTED:** OpenAI exposes `cached_tokens`, and GPT-5.6+ exposes cache-write tokens, specifically enabling cache-read/write monitoring. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
- **DOCUMENTED:** Responses support object metadata consisting of up to 16 key-value pairs, but full memory provenance will usually require application-side tracing. [OpenAI Node response types](https://github.com/openai/openai-node/blob/master/src/resources/responses/responses.ts)
- **INFERRED:** log immutable memory IDs and versions, not only the final prose. Otherwise it is impossible to reconstruct which database state affected a historical answer.
- **INFERRED:** do not put raw sensitive memory in ordinary logs. Store an access-controlled prompt snapshot or content hash plus versioned record references.
- **INFERRED:** calculate cache efficiency as:
  - `cached_tokens / input_tokens`
  - cache-write amortization
  - uncached tokens by template version
  - hit rate by `prompt_cache_key`, task, and deployment.

### Counterfactual design

For a sampled eligible request:

1. run the normal memory-enabled call;
2. asynchronously run the same model snapshot, parameters, stable prompt, and user input with the memory block omitted;
3. do not chain the shadow output into the live conversation;
4. compare both outputs using task-specific deterministic checks and, where needed, a sampled model grader;
5. store the pair under one experiment ID.

- **DOCUMENTED:** OpenAI recommends evals for testing and improving model outputs rather than relying on subjective inspection. [OpenAI evals](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evals)
- **DOCUMENTED:** LangSmith production evaluators support filters and sampling; its documentation gives **10% (`0.1`)** as an example for controlling evaluation cost. [LangSmith online evaluations](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/online-evaluations)
- **INFERRED starting rates:**
  - **1%** of routine high-volume calls;
  - **5%** for new task types or selector revisions;
  - **10%** temporarily during rollout or incident investigation;
  - 100% only for an offline fixed eval set.
- **INFERRED:** stratify sampling by task type and by whether at least one memory was selected. Uniform sampling can miss rare but high-risk task/memory combinations.
- **INFERRED — Cost:** a 1% shadow rate adds approximately **1% of ordinary model-call cost** for the duplicated requests, before grader costs. If outputs are generated to the same length, output-token cost also doubles for that sampled 1%.
- **INFERRED:** save cost by using deterministic outcome checks first and sending only ambiguous pairs to a model grader. Do not reduce shadow output quality so much that the comparison is invalid.
- **INFERRED:** track:
  - memory win rate,
  - no-material-difference rate,
  - regression rate,
  - factual contradiction rate,
  - instruction-violation rate,
  - incremental token cost,
  - quality gain per 1,000 extra memory tokens.

---

# Concrete default configuration

| Setting | Default |
|---|---:|
| Memory block budget | **800 tokens** |
| Optional task-specific ceiling | **1,200 tokens** |
| Ordinary records | **8 max** |
| Pinned records | Included first, but still subject to pinned-budget validation |
| Tokenizer | model mapping via `tiktoken`/`js-tiktoken`; fallback `o200k_base` |
| Token reserve | **max(32 tokens, 5%)** |
| Cache key | `task:<template-id>:<version>` |
| Shadow counterfactual rate | **1% normal, 5% rollout** |
| Selector ordering | scope → task specificity → priority → recency → use → stable ID |
| Memory placement | after stable prompt/examples/tools, before current user input |
| Overflow | drop lowest ordinary records; error if pinned-only block exceeds cap |

These values are **INFERRED starting points**, not vendor limits. Freeze them as versioned configuration and change them only through eval-backed rollout.

# Mistakes that silently cost money or break caching

1. Putting professor memory, user ID, date, nonce, or timestamp at the beginning of the system prompt. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
2. Reordering tool definitions, examples, or memory records nondeterministically. [OpenAI caching cookbook](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/prompt_caching101)
3. Using random `prompt_cache_key` values or one hot key far beyond recommended traffic. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
4. Assuming a stored response or `previous_response_id` means its context is free. Prior chain input remains billable. [OpenAI conversation state](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state)
5. Assuming prior Responses `instructions` carry forward. They explicitly do not. [OpenAI Node response types](https://github.com/openai/openai-node/blob/master/src/resources/responses/responses.ts#L1020-L1027)
6. Appending each memory revision as historical input, leaving contradictory versions in the chain.
7. Counting database text but not the exact serialized wrappers.
8. Using `characters / 4` as a hard multilingual token limit. [tiktoken](https://github.com/openai/tiktoken)
9. Injecting all records merely because they fit the context window; context capacity does not guarantee reliable use. [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)
10. Truncating mandatory policy records silently.
11. Summarizing memory synchronously on every request, adding another model call and unstable prompt bytes.
12. Logging only the rendered memory prose, with no item IDs, versions, selector version, or order.
13. Evaluating memory-enabled outputs without a no-memory counterfactual.
14. Comparing counterfactuals generated with different models, parameters, prompt versions, or conversation state.
15. Treating all GPT-5.x models as having the same cache TTL and write pricing. [OpenAI prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)
